plan.chapterName: Anton, Bivens, and Davis. Calculus, 10th Edition, Figure 14.3.3
plan.contextChunk: This figure shows a polar rectangle R, the fundamental building block for polar double integration. The region R is bounded by two circular arcs r = 1.5 and r = 2 (solid blue curves) and two rays theta = pi/6 and theta = pi/4 (dashed red lines), forming a curved quadrilateral shaded in light blue and labeled R. The figure introduces the polar rectangle as the analogue of the Cartesian rectangle for setting up double integrals in polar coordinates, showing how its curved sides arise from the constant-r and constant-theta boundary conditions.

interactionPlan.concept: A polar rectangle R is the region between two circles of constant radius and two rays of constant angle — the polar-coordinate analogue of a Cartesian rectangle, differing in that its constant-r sides are curved arcs.
elements: polar origin point with a horizontal polar axis (solid black line)
inner circular arc r = 1.5, solid blue, labeled 'r = 1.5'
outer circular arc r = 2, solid blue, labeled 'r = 2'
ray θ = π/6 from the origin, dashed red, labeled
ray θ = π/4 from the origin, dashed red, labeled
polar rectangle R, light blue shaded curved quadrilateral between the two arcs and two rays, labeled 'R'
optional overlaid Cartesian rectangle outline of dimensions Δr × Δθ anchored at the same corner, shown as a straight-edged dashed outline

interactions.label: Inner radius r₁
interactions.teaches: Holding r constant traces a circular arc, so changing r₁ moves the inner curved boundary while the angular extent of R is untouched

interactions.label: Outer radius r₂
interactions.teaches: The radial thickness Δr = r₂ − r₁ of the polar rectangle is set entirely by the two bounding arcs; widening it stretches R outward along every ray

interactions.label: Lower angle θ₁
interactions.teaches: Holding θ constant traces a straight ray from the origin, so rotating θ₁ swings one straight boundary of R while the arcs stay fixed

interactions.label: Upper angle θ₂
interactions.teaches: The angular width Δθ = θ₂ − θ₁ controls how far R sweeps around the origin; the curved sides lengthen as Δθ grows because arc length is r·Δθ

interactions.label: Compare with Cartesian rectangle
interactions.teaches: A Cartesian rectangle with the same Δr × Δθ dimensions has four straight sides, while R's constant-r sides are curved — R is only an analogue of a rectangle, and its true area is not simply Δr·Δθ

demo_steps.title: Anatomy of a polar rectangle
demo_steps.narration: R is bounded by two arcs where r is constant (r = 1.5 and r = 2) and two rays where θ is constant (θ = π/6 and θ = π/4). Four boundary conditions, four sides — just like a rectangle, but in polar coordinates.

demo_steps.title: Radial bounds resize R
demo_steps.narration: Drag r₁ or r₂ and the corresponding arc moves while the rays stay put: the constant-r boundaries are genuinely circular arcs, so R thickens or thins radially.

demo_steps.title: Angular bounds sweep R
demo_steps.narration: Drag θ₁ or θ₂ and the dashed rays rotate: the constant-θ boundaries are straight lines through the origin, and widening Δθ visibly lengthens the curved sides because arc length grows with r·Δθ.

demo_steps.title: Why only an 'analogue'
demo_steps.narration: Overlay the straight-sided rectangle with the same Δr × Δθ: two of R's sides bow outward, so its area is ½(r₂² − r₁²)Δθ, not Δr·Δθ — the source of the extra r in the polar area element dA = r dr dθ.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: A polar rectangle has two straight sides (constant θ) and two curved sides (constant r), which is why its area element is r dr dθ rather than simply dr dθ.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Origin at lower-left with a single horizontal polar axis. Rays dashed red, shallow angles near π/6 and π/4, extending slightly beyond the outer arc. Arcs solid medium-blue, thick strokes, extending slightly past the rays so the boundaries visibly cross. Region R filled light blue with the label 'R' centered inside. Labels in italic serif math styling: 'r = 1.5' above the inner arc, 'r = 2' above the outer arc, 'θ = π/6' and 'θ = π/4' near their rays using stacked fractions. When the overlay toggle is on, draw a thin dashed dark-gray straight-edged rectangle of width Δr and height Δθ anchored at the inner-radius/lower-ray corner of R for direct shape comparison. Sliders update the region, labels, and overlay live; keep r₁ < r₂ and θ₁ < θ₂ enforced.
